column4: The section joins its wording “naʿbudu” (نعبد) to the road; this ayah commands worship of God and names that worship itself “a straight path” (صراط مستقيم), making the two images one relation.
The section sets herd and road together: the passage just described cattle going out to pasture and returning (16:6), and this ayah says the straight route is God’s while some routes deviate (جائر).
The section’s dictionary form “muzallal” (مذلل) joins a subdued camel to a trodden road; here earth is made “dhulūlan” (ذلولًا, subdued/easy) and people are told to walk its paths (مناكبها).
The section’s “hādī” guide and sacrificial herd meet in this ayah: it names the offering (هدي) and says God has guided people (هداكم), while explaining that piety, not flesh or blood, reaches Him.
The section’s wording “those You favored” (أنعمت عليهم) is made concrete here: those who obey God and the Messenger join the prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous whom God favored.

In the section’s night scene Abraham watches the moon set and says that without his Lord’s guidance he would be among the lost; the ayah uses “al-ḍāllīn” (الضالين), the same root/form family as the section’s “lost” ending.
After the star, moon, and sun set in the section’s cited night scene, Abraham turns his face to the Creator of the heavens and earth, distinguishing the rising signs from the Lord they indicate.
The section says a rising sign is not the thing it points to; this ayah explicitly forbids prostration to the sun and moon and commands prostration to God who created them.
The section’s sun-worshippers miss the distinction between sign and Lord; this ayah says the Queen of Sheba’s people prostrate to the sun and that Satan bars them from the way.

This continues 27:24’s sun-worship scene: the ayah asks why they do not prostrate to God, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and earth, completing the section’s sign-versus-signified distinction.
The section contrasts a sign with its Lord; Abraham answers a king’s claim by challenging him to bring the sun from the west after God brings it from the east, exposing the created sun’s limits.

The section brings herd, sacrifice, naming, and submission together; this ayah describes sacrificial camels as among God’s rites, says God’s name is mentioned over them, and calls them made subject to people.
The section places the herd’s pasture journey next to the guidance of 16:9; this ayah specifically names the beauty of livestock when driven out in the morning and brought back in the evening.
The section’s traveler and herd meet in the livestock passage: this ayah says the animals carry people and their loads to a town they could not reach without hardship.
The section joins the herd to the road and a traveler’s mount; this ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys as mounts and adornment.
The section’s road ends at the House; this ayah calls people to pilgrimage to the House from every distant pass, making the route and destination explicit.
This continues the pilgrimage route in 22:27: the ayah’s rites culminate in fulfilling vows and circumambulating the ancient House, the destination in the section’s image.
The section links livestock, naming, and the House; this ayah appoints a rite for every community so they mention God’s name over livestock He provided, then commands submission to Him.
The section’s root/form “rabba” (رَبَّى, to rear) appears in Pharaoh’s claim that he raised Moses as a child; the scene sets a human claimant to nurturing beside Moses’s true Lord.
The section links “Rabb” with raising a child; this prayer asks God for mercy “as they raised me when small” (رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا), directly joining nurture and Lordship.
Moses answers Pharaoh’s charge by saying he acted while among “the lost/unknowing” (الضالين); the section connects this word-family to its final image of being lost from the way.

Immediately after Moses’s “lost” wording in 26:20, he says his Lord gave him judgment and made him a messenger; this is the section’s contrast between Pharaoh’s claimed nurture and the true Lord’s gift.
The section points to Pharaoh’s “favor” claim and the enslavement of Israel in one sentence; this ayah names that forced enslavement, reversing a supposed act of care into oppression.
After the section’s exchange about raising Moses and his Lord’s gifts (26:18–22), Pharaoh asks what the Lord of the worlds is, putting the true Lord at the center of their dispute.
This answers Pharaoh’s question in 26:23: Moses identifies the Lord as Lord of the heavens, earth, and what lies between, enlarging the section’s contrast between a ruler and the true Rabb.
Continuing Moses’s answer in 26:24, this ayah names “your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers,” directly placing Pharaoh himself under the Lord whose nurture he claims.
The section contrasts Pharaoh’s claim to have raised Moses with the true Lord’s care; this ayah recounts Moses being returned to his mother so she could be comforted and not grieve.
The section’s child-rearing image has its other side here: Moses’s mother is told to nurse him, then place him in the river without fear, under God’s promise to return him and make him a messenger.
Pharaoh’s household takes the infant Moses in this ayah, and Pharaoh’s wife asks that he be kept as a child; this supplies the household scene behind Pharaoh’s later claim in 26:18.

This continues Moses’s infancy scene: after he refuses other nurses, his sister directs Pharaoh’s household to his mother, completing the return to nurture that the section sets against Pharaoh’s boast.
The section explicitly joins divine anger to falling: this ayah says whoever incurs God’s anger has “fallen” (هَوَىٰ), a concrete reversal of its upright path and standing images.
Immediately after the fall under wrath in 20:81, this ayah describes the one who repents, believes, and acts rightly as then guided; it supplies the recovery side of the section’s fall/way contrast.
This ayah stages the section’s exact contrast: one walks face-down and the other walks upright on a straight path (سويًا على صراط مستقيم).

The section names this debt passage’s term, witness’s “tadill” (تضلّ, lapse/forget), and “aqwam” (أقوم, more upright); the ayah contrasts a witness’s possible lapse with writing that is more upright and evidentially sound.
The section ties cheating in measure to the day people stand before the Lord; this ayah opens the same passage by condemning those who give short measure.
This continues the short-measure scene of 83:1: the ayah specifies that the cheaters take full measure when others measure for them, sharpening the section’s reversal between taking and giving.
The section points to fraudulent weighing before the day of standing; this ayah completes the fraud by saying they give less when they themselves measure or weigh for others.
This is the section’s stated endpoint for 83:1–3: it names the day people stand before the Lord of the worlds, joining the cheated scale to the reckoning day.
The section brings the scale and people standing on the account day together; this ayah says just scales will be set for the Resurrection and no soul will be wronged.
This ayah makes the section’s weighing image an outcome at judgment: whoever’s scales are heavy has a pleasing life.
This is the other side of 101:6: light scales lead to an abyss, giving the section’s balance a specific boundary between outcomes.
The section joins the heavens and the balance through the root/form “qāma”; this ayah says God raised the heaven and set the balance (الميزان) in the same statement.
This continues the heaven-and-balance image in 55:7: the ayah forbids transgressing in the balance, making its measure an enforceable limit.
Completing 55:7–8, this ayah commands establishing weight with justice and not diminishing the balance, directly meeting the section’s cheating measure.
The section says the judgment-day faces carry a divided outcome; this ayah depicts faces darkened and asks whether they disbelieved after faith, attaching the dark face to punishment.
This is the other face of 3:106: faces are bright and enter God’s mercy, matching the section’s paired faces of wrath and favor.
The section contrasts a softened face with one covered in dust; this ayah gives the positive side as faces “bright” (مُسْفِرَةٌ) on that day.
This gives the section’s dusty face literally: the ayah says dust will be on faces on that day (وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْهَا غَبَرَةٌ).
This completes the dusty faces in 80:40 with darkness covering them, making the judgment-day face a sign of the opposite outcome from the softened one.
The section calls one judgment-day face “nāʿimah” (ناعمة, soft/at ease); this ayah uses the same word for faces enjoying ease that day.
This continues the eased faces of 88:8: they are satisfied with their striving, giving the section’s favorable face a stated cause and response.
The section invokes “the days of God” (أَيَّامِ اللَّهِ) as days of divergent outcomes; here Moses is commanded to remind his people of those days, with signs for the patient and grateful.
The section’s “days of God” frame punishment and forgiveness; this command to believers to pardon those who do not expect God’s days connects those days with forgiving and requital.
The section cites Abraham’s sequence: his Lord created him and “guides me” (يهدين); this ayah gives the guidance link in Abraham’s own account of his Lord.
Continuing 26:78, Abraham says his Lord feeds and gives him drink, the provision that the section places between guidance and hope for forgiveness on the Day of Recompense.
This continues Abraham’s account of his Lord’s care in 26:78–79: he says that when he is ill, God heals him, a specific act of provision on the same path of dependence.
Abraham continues from healing to death and resurrection; this makes the Day of Recompense in 26:82 the end of the life sequence developed by the section.
The section cites Abraham hoping that his Lord forgives him on “the Day of Recompense” (يوم الدين), bringing the section’s Lord, dependence, and reckoning together in the speaker’s own words.
The section’s Moses asks for guidance on the road to Midian; this ayah has him hope that his Lord will guide him to the right way (سواء السبيل).
Continuing Moses’s journey in 28:22, he reaches the well of Midian, where he finds shepherds watering and two women holding back their flock, meeting the section’s road, herd, and water.

After watering the flock in 28:23, Moses withdraws to shade and tells his Lord that he is in need of whatever good is sent down to him; this is the section’s road, water, shelter, and dependence in one scene.
The section’s dictionary forms “neʿāmah” (beam) and “qāmah” (pulley) meet at the well; this ayah explicitly sends a water-drawer down with his bucket into a well.
The section says the road has an arrival house; this ayah says God calls to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path.
The section’s recap names cloud and vegetation among the Lord’s gifts; this ayah says God sends down rainwater for people to drink and for plants to grow.
Continuing the rain in 16:10, this ayah names crops, olives, palms, grapes, and other fruits as growing from it, making provision visible in the land.
The section joins cloud, rain, and the Lord nurturing plants; this ayah describes winds carrying heavy clouds, rain sent to a dead land, and fruit brought forth from it.
This ayah describes God sending winds as glad tidings before mercy and sending down pure water, directly meeting the section’s cloud-and-provision image.
Continuing the rain in 25:48, this ayah says the water revives a dead land and gives drink to livestock and people, completing the section’s cloud-to-herd provision.
The section’s cloud image is staged here: God sends winds that stir clouds, spreads them across the sky, and sends rain from them.
This continues 30:48’s rain: the ayah tells the Prophet to look at the traces of God’s mercy in how He revives the earth after its death.
The section says the Lord nurtures plants through clouds and rain; this ayah says water is sent down in due measure and kept on earth, making provision measured rather than ownerless.
Continuing the measured water in 23:18, this ayah names gardens of palms and grapes and fruits as its yield, connecting rain to completed provision.
The section joins the womb to the Lord who forms and raises; this ayah begins a specific sequence of human creation from clay and then a drop placed in a secure lodging.
This continues 23:12’s creation sequence by locating the drop in the womb, the section’s explicit image of nurture and formation.
This completes the womb sequence from 23:12–13 through staged formation to a new creation, matching the section’s growth toward completion.
The section joins the womb, nurture, and a completed blessing; this ayah traces a mother’s bearing and weaning to the child reaching maturity, then has the person ask to be grateful for God’s favor.
This ayah says people are brought from their mothers’ wombs knowing nothing and given hearing, sight, and hearts, a direct account of the womb and the Lord’s provision after birth.
The section’s phrase “completion of favor” meets this ayah’s explicit “I have perfected My favor upon you” (أَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِي), identifying completion as a divine gift.
This ayah says the Book was given to Moses to complete God’s favor upon the good-doer and as guidance and mercy, bringing the section’s Moses, completed gift, and path together.
The section asks for the straight path of those favored; this ayah names prophets and righteous people whom God chose and guided to a straight path.
The section’s wording “those You favored” (أنعمت عليهم) has a concrete parallel in the prophets God favored; this ayah shows them falling in prostration when the Merciful’s signs are recited.
This begins the section’s night sequence: Abraham watches a star set and rejects it as Lord when it disappears, treating the celestial body as a sign rather than the Creator.
After the star and moon in 6:76–77, Abraham watches the sun set and says he is clear of the people’s association, completing the section’s sequence of fading celestial signs.
This immediately introduces Abraham’s night scene by saying God showed him the dominion of the heavens and earth so he could be certain, supplying the created order behind the signs.
The section’s “Owner of the Day of Recompense” makes ownership central to judgment; this ayah asks whose dominion is that day and answers that it belongs to God alone.
The section’s “Day of Recompense” is stated explicitly here as “what is the Day of Recompense?” (وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ), opening the account-day scene.
This repeats and emphasizes the question in 82:17 about the Day of Recompense, giving the section’s named day a distinct boundary before its answer.
This answers the repeated question in 82:17–18: no soul can avail another on that day, and command belongs to God, directly meeting the section’s ownership and reckoning.
The section’s term “yawm al-dīn” (يوم الدين) is explicit here as the day on which recompense occurs (لَوَاقِعٌ), a direct parallel to its account day.
The section’s Day of Recompense is named here when the deniers exclaim that it is the Day of Judgment, making the reckoning scene explicit.
The section moves from the known owner to the day property is gathered under one ruler; this ayah says dominion belongs to God and that He gives and takes it as He wills.
The section’s recap names the Lord who feeds clouds and plants; this ayah pairs the sky as canopy with rain sent down and fruits brought forth as provision.
This ayah gathers heaven and earth, winds, clouds, and rain that revives the earth into signs, closely matching the section’s linked cloud-and-growth image.
This continues the moving clouds in 30:48: people rejoice when rain descends, adding the recipient’s response to the section’s provided rain.
The section’s rain-and-growth image is stated here as God sending winds that raise clouds and reviving the earth after its death, a sign of resurrection as well as provision.
This ayah sends water down and grows crops of varied colors, then shows them yellowing and becoming debris; it joins the section’s provision image to the limit of what grows.
The section’s road and cloud-to-plant images meet in this ayah: God makes earth a cradle, lays out paths, sends water from heaven, and brings out varied vegetation.
This restates the section’s road image as God making earth a cradle and making paths in it so people may be guided.
The section’s path begins on land; this ayah says God spread the earth out for people, preparing the ground they travel over.
Continuing 71:19, this ayah says people may travel through broad paths in the earth, directly joining land and way.
This ayah says God set mountains, rivers, and paths on earth so people may be guided, joining the landscape and wayfinding images in the section.
Continuing the landmarks and paths in 16:15, this ayah says people are guided by landmarks and stars, meeting the section’s guide for travelers and herd.
The section’s “hādī” guide for the traveler meets this ayah’s stars, made as guidance through the darknesses of land and sea.
This ayah asks who guides people in the darknesses of land and sea and sends winds before mercy, joining the section’s wayfinding and cloud/rain scenes.
The section distinguishes the straight path from deviation; this ayah commands following God’s one straight path and forbids following other paths that divide people from it.
The section presents worship as chosen service on the path; this neighboring command forbids serving Satan and calls him a clear enemy, setting a contrary master beside God.
The section’s dictionary form “muzallal” (مذلل) is a tamed camel; this cow is specifically said not to plow earth or water a field, a boundary case for an animal’s being made useful or subdued.
The section joins voluntary service to travel on a mount; this ayah has riders remember that God subjected these animals and give thanks for the mount carrying them.
The section’s herds and owner-language meet this ayah’s cattle made by God’s hands and placed under human control, with people as their owners and users.
The section portrays a weary traveler needing guidance and help; Moses and his companion here say their journey has brought them fatigue, a concrete road-weariness parallel.
The section links Moses’s “lost” wording in 26:20 to his past; in this separate account he admits he wronged himself after striking a man and asks his Lord to forgive him.
Continuing Moses’s admission in 28:15, this ayah says God forgave him, a specific instance of the Lord’s gift after his error.
This completes the dusty faces of 80:40–41 by identifying them as disbelievers and wicked-doers, giving the section’s adverse face a stated moral outcome.
The section’s paired judgment faces include one softened and one under dust; this ayah describes faces humbled on that day, the adverse posture that contrasts with 88:8’s ease.
This continues the humbled faces in 88:2: they are laboring and exhausted, making the adverse face an embodied condition alongside the section’s ease-filled face.
This ayah gives the bright side of the section’s judgment-day faces: some faces that day are radiant, looking toward their Lord.
This ayah sets frowning faces beside the radiant faces of 75:22, a specific facial reversal on the same judgment day.

The section’s sign-and-mark image distinguishes an outward sign from what it indicates; this ayah describes a mark on believers’ faces from prostration, a specific mark that points to a devotional history.
The section places standing and a balance on the account day; this ayah says those whose scales are heavy will succeed, stating the favorable result of that image.
This is the adverse outcome paired with 23:102: those whose scales are light have lost themselves, connecting the section’s balance to loss.
The section joins measure to reckoning; this ayah says weighing on that day is truth, making the scale a standard for judgment.
This gives the opposite result in 7:8: those whose scales are light have lost themselves, joining the section’s measure to a way lost.
The section names the balance and fraud in measurement; this command pairs full measure with a straight balance (مستقيم), making upright measure a concrete duty.

The section links the scale to people standing upright; this ayah says Scripture and the balance were sent so people might uphold justice (ليقوم الناس بالقسط), connecting the balance to q-w-m, “stand/establish.”
The section’s Lord completes gifts; this ayah says God has given people from all they asked, yet they could not count His favor, making abundance and its uncountability explicit.
This repeats the section’s idea of completed favor as a gift beyond counting: if people tried to count God’s favors, they could not enumerate them.
The section names the Lord’s gifts as visible and hidden; this ayah says God has subjected what is in the heavens and earth and poured His favors over people, both apparent and concealed.
The section includes the womb as a place of divine forming; this ayah says God shapes people in wombs as He wills.
This ayah names creation in mothers’ wombs through three layers of darkness, a specific womb image connected to the section’s formative care.
This ayah describes womb development through stages until a stated term and maturity, a concrete parallel to the section’s growth toward completion.
This ayah traces human growth from a drop to maturity and old age, linking the section’s womb and child-rearing images to development over time.
This ayah recalls a mother carrying and weaning a child and commands gratitude to God and parents, connecting the section’s nurturing image to thankfulness for favor.
God tells Moses He has already bestowed another favor on him, introducing the infancy account that follows and the section’s theme of gifts beyond Pharaoh’s claimed nurture.
This continues the favor in 20:37 by recalling the revelation to Moses’s mother, part of the care that preserved the infant before Pharaoh’s household took him.
Continuing the infancy account, Moses is placed in a chest and the river carries him to the bank; this supplies the concrete preservation behind God’s favor in 20:37.
This continues 28:7: Pharaoh’s household picks up the infant Moses, setting up the human foster-care claim that the section reads against God’s care.
This completes Moses’s return to his mother in 28:12; the ayah says God restored him to her so she could be comforted and know God’s promise was true.
This is Pharaoh’s accusation immediately before Moses’s answer in 26:20: he calls the deed an act and Moses ungrateful, giving the “lost” reply its debate context.
This continues the exchange about the Lord of the worlds: Pharaoh addresses the surrounding chiefs after Moses identifies the Lord, showing his rejection of the answer.
Pharaoh calls Moses mad after Moses names the Lord of the worlds; this is a concrete hostile response within the section’s contrast between false ruler and true Rabb.
Moses answers that the Lord of the east and west and what lies between them is the true Lord, extending the section’s distinction between created signs and their Lord.
Pharaoh threatens to imprison Moses after the Lord-of-worlds exchange, turning his claim to authority into coercion, as in the section’s contrast between service and enslavement.
After Pharaoh asks who their Lord is, this ayah gives the question that leads to Moses’s answer about God giving each thing its form and guidance in 20:50.
Moses says his Lord gave everything its form and then guided it; the section joins the Lord who forms and nurtures with the guide who leads on a path.
Moses says his Lord neither errs nor forgets (لَا يَضِلُّ رَبِّي وَلَا يَنْسَى); this gives a specific contrast to the section’s witness who may “tadill” (تضلّ, lapse) in 2:282.
This ayah says people were created from earth, returned to it, and brought forth again, linking the section’s earth, death, and account-day images.
The section’s willing servant addresses one Lord; this command has Muhammad say he was ordered to worship God sincerely in religion, a specific speaker stance of chosen service.
This continues the sincere worship statement: Muhammad says he worships God alone, echoing the section’s direct address to its sole master.
The section says the owned person turns willingly to the owner; this ayah has the speaker say his prayer, sacrifice, life, and death belong to God, Lord of the worlds.
The section links a herd offering to the House; this ayah names the Kaaba, the Sacred House, as a place of standing for people and names sacrificial offerings among its sacred markers.
The section’s road has an arrival House; this ayah identifies the House as a place of return and safety and commands Abraham and Ishmael to purify it for worshippers.
Abraham and Ishmael raise the House’s foundations and ask God to accept their work, joining the section’s Ibrahim, House, and worship images.
This continues the pilgrimage call: it says to mention God’s name over livestock He provided on appointed days, then eat and feed the needy.
This continues the sacrificial-animal passage: livestock have benefits until an appointed term, and their destination is the ancient House.
The section says the herd is named for God before sacrifice; this ayah commands eating from livestock over which God’s name has been mentioned.
This is the boundary of 6:118’s named offering: the ayah forbids eating from what has not had God’s name mentioned, linking the section’s naming detail to a clear limit.
This begins the section’s herd passage: livestock supply warmth, benefits, and food, giving concrete content to the Lord’s provision.
This ayah recalls God’s deliverance of Israel from Pharaoh and His meeting promise to Moses, a neighboring account of rescue from the false ruler described in the section.
Pharaoh boasts that Egypt and its rivers belong to him; this concrete claim to possession contrasts with the section’s true Lord and the ruler who falsely claims to have raised Moses.
This says Pharaoh misled his people and they obeyed him, a specific instance of a human leader diverting a people from the way under the section’s false-master theme.
This ayah says the deniers will enter the Fire on the Day of Recompense, giving a specific adverse outcome for the day named in the section.
This continues 82:15 by saying they will not be absent from it, making the judgment consequence lasting.
This ayah identifies those who deny the Day of Recompense, a specific opposing stance to the section’s account day.
The condemned speakers say they denied the Day of Recompense; this is a direct contrary stance to the section’s reckoning day, though the ayah does not stage its balance or faces.
The section pairs judgment with approval and anger; this ayah addresses the tranquil soul, a specific inner state that prepares the return to its Lord in the following verses.
This completes 89:27’s address by inviting the soul to return to its Lord pleased and pleasing, a concrete meeting of the section’s Lord and favor.
Before Abraham’s night scene, he challenges his father for taking idols as gods; this supplies the rejection of false lords behind the section’s distinction between sign and Lord.
The section’s Abraham considers celestial bodies before rejecting them as Lords; this ayah also depicts him looking toward the stars in a separate scene, a specific but less direct parallel.
The section says a sign is distinct from what it points to; this ayah speaks of signs on the horizons and within people until truth is clear, a specific sign-to-reality parallel.
This completes the Sheba passage’s corrective to sun-worship: God alone is God and Lord of the mighty throne, naming the Lord whom the sign should point toward.
After naming prophets guided to a straight path in 6:87, this ayah says that is God’s guidance, supporting the section’s requested guidance for the favored community.
This ayah describes revelation as bringing people from darkness into light by their Lord’s permission and to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy, a specific guidance-to-path formulation.
The section pairs wrath with a lost way; this ayah says wrath and humiliation will overtake those who took the calf, a specific scene of divine anger after idolatry.
This ayah names God’s anger against hypocritical men and women and associators, a specific parallel to the section’s category of those under wrath.
This ayah asks whether messengers came from among jinn and humans to warn of meeting this day, joining the section’s account day to being warned and addressed.
This ayah says God sends water from the sky and revives the earth after its death, a specific water-and-life parallel to the section’s cloud-fed vegetation.
This ayah describes the earth as humble and then stirred into growth by rain; it joins the section’s subdued ground, rain, and plant images.
This ayah says God sends pouring water from clouds, directly naming the cloud-to-rain image in the section’s account of provision.
The water in 78:14 produces grain and plants here, completing a specific cloud-to-food sequence.
This continues the plants of 78:15 with thick gardens, extending the section’s rain-fed provision to its visible completion.
This ayah shows rain making vegetation grow and then becoming dry debris scattered by the wind, a specific parallel to provision that passes away.

The section contrasts the known owner with people whose status differs by reverence; this ayah says the most honored before God is the most God-conscious, a specific limit on human ownership or lineage.
This ayah names nursing a child for two full years and the parents’ duty to provide, a specific continuation of the section’s child-rearing image.
The section contrasts face-down stumbling with upright walking on the straight path; this ayah says those gathered on their faces to Hell are worse in destination and more astray.
This ayah describes people gathered on their faces on the Day of Resurrection, a specific adverse reversal of the section’s upright traveler.
This ayah says those under God’s curse and anger are made apes and swine, a specific outcome for the section’s category of those under wrath.
The section’s final camel is detached from its owner; this ayah has prized pregnant camels abandoned at the upheaval, a concrete but uncertain parallel because the reason for abandonment differs.
